newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech IPS shares rated sell - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Czech IPS shares rated sell - analysts.

text.p: Shares in the largest Czech construction firm IPS Praha a.s. are heavily overvalued because of much worse than expected 1996 profit figures and investors are advised to sell, analysts said.

IPS rose one crown to 276 on the Prague bourse on Thursday but it has declined sharply in recent sessions from a year high of 327 in late February. The company's 1996 price earnings ratio, based on the preliminary results, was around 40.
Analysts said the root of their concern about IPS lay in the huge gap between management's predictions for 1996 profits and preliminary unaudited results for last year which were released on March 7.

"...reported preliminary unaudited results, showing a drop in net profit in 1996 of 45 percent to CZK 91 million came as an unpleasant surprise," said a report to investors on IPS by ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.
"They are at odds with management forecasts released on 14 November 1996 predicting that net profit would increase to CZK 182 million."
Based on its concerns, ABN AMRO Hoare Govett downgraded its recommendation from hold to sell.
Pavel Sobisek, chief analyst at Zivnostenska Banka, agreed:
"We can expect another phase of price falls which means we recommend selling (shares in) the company."
The declining fortunes of IPS come at a difficult time for the Czech construction industry as a whole.
On Wednesday, the Czech Statistical Office said that construction output fell 18.6 percent year-on-year in January compared with a 5.7 percent drop in December.

But despite the sector-wide problems, the ABN AMRO Hoare Govett report focused on the management of the company itself, especially its record on assessing the risk attached to outstanding receivables.
Bad debts on a series of subcontracting operations ended with write-offs of 50 million crowns.

"The absence of any provisions or warning in the (profit) forecasts issued on November 14 suggest that at that stage management was unaware of the problem, or else had unrealistic expectations of the likelihood of the company's being paid."
